title: Neural networks are clean
author: themgt
relevanceReason: 命中 5 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: The Short VersionI think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean.There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability. The first is rapid normal science on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original.The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots. We had canonical examples of polysemantic neurons, the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand. The most famous one, in an image model, responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. And the last layer of the early field’s model organism, InceptionV1, seemed so full of arbitrary mixtures it wasn’t clear how to study it: almost none of the neurons were easily interpretable.The leading explanation for polysemanticity was superposition. This proposed a new learning principle: when a neural network runs out of neurons, it stops grouping related things together and instead begins folding unrelated things together, simply because they don’t interfere. The result is a kind of knot: the network could have folded in many almost equally good ways, so which things a neuron groups together tells you almost nothing. You have to unfold the knot before you can study anything. In practice that means training a second model – a decomposition such as a sparse autoencoder – to approximate the network as it would look unfolded and studying that instead. If the network really is knotted, there may be no alternative.One main result is that superposition was the wrong explanation for InceptionV1. Architectural problems made later layers overflow. Weak interpretability tools amplified these problems, making the late layers seem incoherent. Since then, architectural changes designed to help deep layers learn better have had the unintended effect of making them more interpretable. When we first studied InceptionV1, we found almost no interpretable neurons in its last layer. But with these ordinary improvements, and no change to model size or training data, 99-100% of neurons in that last layer are easily interpretable and the model is broadly legible the whole way through. It’s the first non-trivial neural network I feel I mostly understand; you can browse it here. I trained versions of it across a 300× range in size, and it’s broadly legible at every scale. With less room, the network doesn’t fold unrelated things together; its neurons just cover coarser-grained concepts, like one car neuron covering many kinds of car. With more room, that neuron differentiates into many specific cars. So the problem wasn’t the presence of a second learning principle, it was just an ordinary learning failure of the first one, and it’s easy to fix.The canonical vision examples of polysemanticity and superposition were errors too. In 2019, Chris Olah and I found the circuit that was originally introduced as the superposition phenomenon in Zoom InZoom In: An Introduction to CircuitsOlah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓. It showed a car feature appearing to spread into a set of unrelated dog neurons. It was the only one we showed, and the only one I ever saw. We read it as the network placing the car in a high-dimensional hiding place, for downstream neurons to read back out. But nothing reads that combination. It wasn’t hiding anything; it was ordinary generalization and composition. To my knowledge, no one has published a second circuit with the right shape.Modern language models are also far more interpretable than generally believed. Anthropic’s Towards MonosemanticityTowards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary LearningBricken, T., Templeton, A., Batson, J., et al., 2023. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ (2023), studying a small one-layer model, gave the median neuron a 0 on its rubric out of a possible 14, meaning the rater couldn’t form any hypothesis. The automated interpretability projectLanguage Models Can Explain Neurons in Language ModelsBills, S., Cammarata, N., Mossing, D., et al., 2023. OpenAI. References ↓ I started at OpenAI (also 2023) found about 1.7% of neurons interpretable by our most generous measure.With better tools and modern models, the situation looks quite different. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understoodA note on this number: the share of neurons with one job varies depending on how you set the threshold for counting weak activations, depth, density of sub-circuits, and what you view as “one thing”.How far to go into weak activations is a big factor here. There’s a section describing weak activations below. It tends to increase how many “related things” there are, more than whether the neuron is a judgement of something legible. For instance, the Trump neuron’s weak activations bring in MAGA hats and people related to him. The Titanic neuron’s weak activations bring in stories of more general voyages, or steam engines and other technologies of the era.There’s also the question of whether to care about activation percentiles, or fraction of the strongest activations. In general I think what the neuron learns should be trusted, its natural sparsity and activation ranges and so on. Which I used to mostly not believe! I’m somewhat against trying to standardize things across all neurons. Percentiles are more common today, I think because they’re easier to think about.It goes the other way too. For instance, when you look at the Titanic neuron’s “unrelated jobs,” it’s often detecting that “boat” comes next. The tool missed this because it only looked backward when judging context. When we look at these “unrelated jobs” in depth, it’s almost always this kind of thing. It’s easy to build an imperfect tool.Overall, I don’t think coming to a single score is actually that important. But when it was taken out, early reviewers felt unanchored without even a rough number. In the sets I’ve looked at more closely, considering strong activations, it’s closer to 97% non-arbitrary mixtures, but these are relatively small samples.Overall distilling everything into one “cleanliness” score should be taken as a broad pointer to the regime a neural network is in, rather than something precise to either optimize directly or hold too tightly. A lot of this essay is for being less dimensionality reduced, treating each neuron and circuit differently, according to their motifs, depth, role etc. Despite this, a rough number can be useful.. Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail. These percentages compress a high-dimensional picture into a few numbers, and the precise number depends on where you set thresholds for what counts as “one thing” – like whether you lump together closely related idioms in two languages. I don’t think much in interpretability hangs on that question. What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place.Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. This idea first appeared in a forgotten subsection of a paper I worked on called Multimodal NeuronsMultimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural NetworksGoh, G., Cammarata, N., Voss, C., et al., 2021. Distill. References ↓ (2021). At the time, I hadn’t watched neurons grow over training. Now it’s easier, and it holds up everywhere I’ve seen. Even the original InceptionV1 wasn’t knotted. When I retrain its original architecture, which still produces messy deep layers, and follow the least legible neurons I can find, they turn out to be overgrowing locally into reasonable, adjacent territory.So there were two explanations for polysemanticity, and I helped propose both. In some ways, they’re opposites: generalization groups similar things together and superposition groups unrelated things together. Superposition is the one the field bet on and, until recently, so did I. But I now think recursive generalization was basically right. That leaves one learning principle after all. It’s still generalization, but it turns out generalization is fractal. That’s far less concerning: there’s something to learn from the way things were grouped, and nothing to learn from two items in superposition. And since the generalization itself is fractal, our explanations can be too: start with a basic explanation, then zoom in when you want to understand more. In that sense, almost the entire network is interpretable if we look closely enough, especially if we look at how it grew over training.Why was the gap so large? I think several ordinary problems compounded. The explainer models of 2023 couldn’t run the loop of conjecture and test; the tools and metrics were weak, rewarding explanations that could simulate activations rather than ones that were right, which often come apart; no one knew what language neuron motifs to expect, and people broadly looked for the wrong kinds of things; and most studies used small or simplified models. In a sense, those models really had run out of room, which made superposition the natural explanation. But a network short on room doesn’t switch learning principles; its neurons just get broader, as in the small vision models. Broad neurons are usually easy to break down once you know what to look for. Without that knowledge, and with primitive tools, they look like arbitrary mixtures.Interpretability has a surprising amount of momentum: like a jigsaw puzzle or crossword, any understanding you gain starts constraining the rest of the system. At first, you’re looking at a single neuron. If you can’t understand it, little else helps: circuits and attribution graphs only explain a neuron in terms of other neurons you don’t understand yet. This can make getting started hard. Once the map starts to fill in, though, it goes surprisingly well. If you don’t understand exactly what a neuron does, you can study what it connects to, the ecosystem around it, and – in a mixture-of-experts model – what its expert specializes in. As with a puzzle coming together, every piece comes with many clues, and they’re well structured and easy to run experiments against. That’s why nearly empty and mostly filled in aren’t surprising places to be; they’re the natural anchors.Take a neuron that tracks ‘a sense of righteousness when a bargain purchase turns out to work better than the expensive alternative’. Neurons that track a feeling or social cue like this are some of the most common we’ve found. Imagine finding this one with no knowledge of language neuron motifs and no circuits to lean on, because few neighboring neurons are explained yet. Most humans and agents expect neurons to detect nouns by firing on them, which they mostly don’t. Look at where this one fires most strongly, and you see a pile of seemingly unrelated commas.Now imagine the map is mostly filled in. You know many neurons detect subtle feelings or social contexts, and that they often fire not on the words that carry the feeling but on punctuation, like commas, where the model summarizes what a sentence meant, or on the word just before the feeling matters for predicting what comes next. So you read the surrounding sentences instead, and check its steering effects (what the model writes when you turn the neuron up), which line up closely. You look upstream at how it’s built and downstream at what it does, and both line up. You check its negative pole, what pushes it strongly negative, and find a subtle variant of the same cue, or the moment the social context ends. You can run specific tests, like checking which store brands it responds to. Any of these could break the explanation, yet they keep pointing to the same place. And understanding this neuron sharpens the broader motif: after thousands of subtle-feeling and social-context detectors, you start to know what to expect from the next one, which is part of why the map fills in faster as it goes.It works on the tools too. When you can see 2% of a network, you can’t tell where your tools are broken; when you can see most of it, the unexplained remainder points straight at them. That’s how some coworkers and I found a double-negative regime in SwiGLU neurons that, as far as we know, no one had noticed, and that a decomposition mixing many neurons together would likely have hidden.The bad news about modern neural networks is that they're enormous. The good news is that the enormity helps: as the map fills in, every explanation is tightly constrained by everything around it, and bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize in the first place.In this sense, understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most. First, it’s hard to know how to think like a neural network until you’ve studied it closely. For instance, “deception” is a useful initial frame, but the building blocks that contribute to deceptive behavior by models probably have alignment-relevant microstructure that will be hard to know without going in and looking. Second, targeting a small set of mechanisms is like working on one row of an otherwise empty crossword. It’s doable, and might work, but without the crossings it’s hard to know whether you’re right. It may be easier to solve the whole thing – or at least the broader parts of the network these mechanisms connect to.When I ran this process on modern convolutional networks, it basically worked. Agents can map out neurons and circuits, build explorable microscopes and explore them, test explanations thoroughly, and track hundreds of thousands of attribution graphs. There was never a point where rapid normal science broke down. I now feel I basically understand these models, at least enough to know where I’d start asking any question I had; eventually, the crossword just got filled in. So far it has worked in language models too, up to trillions of parameters. Those aren’t close to solved due to sheer size, but I’m optimistic about scaling the process.All of this has brought me back to an old hope: understanding a neural network directly, by studying its mechanisms and the data flowing between them, without first trying to fix or untangle it. Put together, the argument has four steps.Networks use one learning principle, not two (if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn’t matter for study), so there’s no blocker to beginning ordinary science on them.With modern models and tools, that science goes much better than most people expect.Understanding compounds, so it gets easier as the map fills in. At minimum, then, a network’s own mechanisms should be part of the toolkit.Highly speculative: this might be most of what we need, and interpretability might be far more tractable, possibly in the near term, than we’ve assumed.That’s been the pattern for deep learning in general: the simple thing at absurd scale beats the clever one. Rich Sutton called it the bitter lessonThe Bitter LessonSutton, R., 2019. Incomplete Ideas. References ↓. Maybe there’s a bitter lesson for interpretability too: scaling ordinary investigation beats engineering a clever new decomposition.A technical companion paper will offer a more detailed account of language model neuron experiments, such as what we’ve found about the different regimes of modern non-linearities and what kinds of circuit motifs show up at different depths. This essay glances at many places and conjectures about where it all might be pointing.Cars and AnimalsThe most famous polysemantic neuron is 4e:55 of InceptionV1, which looked like an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars. It’s been brought up as evidence that neurons might not be the right unit of study in several of the field’s most widely read papers, from Feature VisualizationFeature VisualizationOlah, C., Mordvintsev, A. and Schubert, L., 2017. Distill. References ↓ in 2017 to Zoom InZoom In: An Introduction to CircuitsOlah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓. In Zoom In, which I co-authored, we said outright that it “isn’t responding to some commonality of cars and cat faces”.In Multimodal Neurons we came very close. We asked whether the neuron might be responding to some shared feature, “perhaps cat eyes and car lights look similar,” then decided from the feature visualization’s whiskers and chrome that it was “genuinely OR(cat, car).” We were right to look for a shared shape, but I think we underestimated how far generalization reaches. The shared feature was the V. I think the whiskers misled us because generalization happens inside high-level patterns. The V neuron really does take in cat circuitry, and feature visualization’s job is to raise the activation, so once it finds the cat route it adds everything that route brings. The whiskers come along for the ride, even if the neuron doesn’t “want” them. Downstream, the car readers do get a little cat signal through the V neuron, but it barely reaches the output: one cat detector firing does little on its own, since many work together, so the network never needs a negative weight to cancel it. To see the shared pattern, you have to visualize what the neuron’s inputs have in common, not the neuron on its own.After months of seeing clean neurons, I wondered if we’d misinterpreted some early prominent examples of polysemanticity and superposition. The canonical polysemantic neuron seemed like the obvious place to check, so I opened up the cat and car image grid I’d seen hundreds of times before and did something I’d never done: I spent a few seconds wondering what one thing this might be. Almost instantly it was obvious: it’s not a cat and car neuron, it’s a V-shape neuron.I looked at its circuit connections: V-shaped flames, V-shaped water jets from a fireboat, V-shaped fox faces. I looked at its negative pole: an O, round where the V is pointed. Why would an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars need to connect so strongly to a flame?

Then I went to the canonical superposition circuit I first found in 2019I found it while building my first Circuits interface, which only had feature visualization and weights connecting their neurons. Then I took them to Chris Olah and asked why the car would be going into these dogs like this. We came to the conclusion it must be doing a kind of folding, and called it superposition. It was an intuitive explanation for what we saw, so it didn’t prompt diving more into the tools, which would have revealed feature visualization reward hacking and various other things. It being placed into a high-dimensional space felt like a reasonable answer.. The V neuron and this circuit were Zoom InZoom In: An Introduction to CircuitsOlah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓’s two main examples of why its picture of neurons, that nearly every one turns out to be understandable if you look seriously, might be “overly rosy”.The circuit appeared to show a car going into a bunch of unrelated dogs, as if the dogs were a kind of high-dimensional storage place where the car could be recovered later as needed.But that’s not what the car was doing. Cars and dogs were being brought together because of shared pose. InceptionV1 has more than a hundred of these generalized pose neurons, each one its own clean detector of a pose shared across cars, dogs and other objects, and to my knowledge no one had noticed them. Later layers keep building on them, all the way to the end of the model. The car was not being stored in an obscure place, and nothing directly reads out the combination. It’s the opposite: it’s continuing to differentiate into car specialists and finer poses.Part of the reason was not knowing about generalized pose neurons, and part of the reason is that the technique we use to render icons of images — feature visualization — ends up being reward hacked in deeper layers. The intent is to find an image that maximizes the neuron, but the way that’s done is through gradient descent, and it takes the easiest path, which in InceptionV1 often means dogs. There are lots of dogs in InceptionV1’s training data and a lot of dog neurons, and the early optimization falls into them and never recovers. If you even lightly bias it toward the natural paths the top images take, most of them are cars, and some are both dogs and cars, because of shared pose.

And understanding this neuron sharpens the broader motif: after thousands of subtle-feeling and social-context detectors, you start to know what to expect from the next one, which is part of why the map fills in faster as it goes.It works on the tools too. When you can see 2% of a network, you can’t tell where your tools are broken; when you can see most of it, the unexplained remainder points straight at them. That’s how some coworkers and I found a double-negative regime in SwiGLU neurons that, as far as we know, no one had noticed, and that a decomposition mixing many neurons together would likely have hidden.The bad news about modern neural networks is that they're enormous. The good news is that the enormity helps: as the map fills in, every explanation is tightly constrained by everything around it, and bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize in the first place.In this sense, understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most. First, it’s hard to know how to think like a neural network until you’ve studied it closely. For instance, “deception” is a useful initial frame, but the building blocks that contribute to deceptive behavior by models probably have alignment-relevant microstructure that will be hard to know without going in and looking. Second, targeting a small set of mechanisms is like working on one row of an otherwise empty crossword. It’s doable, and might work, but without the crossings it’s hard to know whether you’re right. It may be easier to solve the whole thing – or at least the broader parts of the network these mechanisms connect to.When I ran this process on modern convolutional networks, it basically worked. Agents can map out neurons and circuits, build explorable microscopes and explore them, test explanations thoroughly, and track hundreds of thousands of attribution graphs. There was never a point where rapid normal science broke down. I now feel I basically understand these models, at least enough to know where I’d start asking any question I had; eventually, the crossword just got filled in. So far it has worked in language models too, up to trillions of parameters. Those aren’t close to solved due to sheer size, but I’m optimistic about scaling the process.All of this has brought me back to an old hope: understanding a neural network directly, by studying its mechanisms and the data flowing between them, without first trying to fix or untangle it. Put together, the argument has four steps.Networks use one learning principle, not two (if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn’t matter for study), so there’s no blocker to beginning ordinary science on them.With modern models and tools, that science goes much better than most people expect.Understanding compounds, so it gets easier as the map fills in. At minimum, then, a network’s own mechanisms should be part of the toolkit.Highly speculative: this might be most of what we need, and interpretability might be far more tractable, possibly in the near term, than we’ve assumed.That’s been the pattern for deep learning in general: the simple thing at absurd scale beats the clever one. Rich Sutton called it the bitter lessonThe Bitter LessonSutton, R., 2019. Incomplete Ideas. References ↓. Maybe there’s a bitter lesson for interpretability too: scaling ordinary investigation beats engineering a clever new decomposition.A technical companion paper will offer a more detailed account of language model neuron experiments, such as what we’ve found about the different regimes of modern non-linearities and what kinds of circuit motifs show up at different depths. This essay glances at many places and conjectures about where it all might be pointing.Cars and AnimalsThe most famous polysemantic neuron is 4e:55 of InceptionV1, which looked like an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars. It’s been brought up as evidence that neurons might not be the right unit of study in several of the field’s most widely read papers, from Feature VisualizationFeature VisualizationOlah, C., Mordvintsev, A. and Schubert, L., 2017. Distill. References ↓ in 2017 to Zoom InZoom In: An Introduction to CircuitsOlah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓. In Zoom In, which I co-authored, we said outright that it “isn’t responding to some commonality of cars and cat faces”.In Multimodal Neurons we came very close. We asked whether the neuron might be responding to some shared feature, “perhaps cat eyes and car lights look similar,” then decided from the feature visualization’s whiskers and chrome that it was “genuinely OR(cat, car).” We were right to look for a shared shape, but I think we underestimated how far generalization reaches. The shared feature was the V. I think the whiskers misled us because generalization happens inside high-level patterns. The V neuron really does take in cat circuitry, and feature visualization’s job is to raise the activation, so once it finds the cat route it adds everything that route brings. The whiskers come along for the ride, even if the neuron doesn’t “want” them. Downstream, the car readers do get a little cat signal through the V neuron, but it barely reaches the output: one cat detector firing does little on its own, since many work together, so the network never needs a negative weight to cancel it. To see the shared pattern, you have to visualize what the neuron’s inputs have in common, not the neuron on its own.After months of seeing clean neurons, I wondered if we’d misinterpreted some early prominent examples of polysemanticity and superposition. The canonical polysemantic neuron seemed like the obvious place to check, so I opened up the cat and car image grid I’d seen hundreds of times before and did something I’d never done: I spent a few seconds wondering what one thing this might be. Almost instantly it was obvious: it’s not a cat and car neuron, it’s a V-shape neuron.I looked at its circuit connections: V-shaped flames, V-shaped water jets from a fireboat, V-shaped fox faces. I looked at its negative pole: an O, round where the V is pointed. Why would an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars need to connect so strongly to a flame?

comments.author: sebmellen
comments.textRawHtml:
Nick is a force of nature. Highly recommend following him on X if you don't already.

His launch post gives good context not found in the blog:

> interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

> with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

children.author: kyle-rb
children.textRawHtml:
The more obvious bias is towards Premium subscribers over us freeloaders. The reply-ranking algorithm was a nightmare for a while; they strictly adhered to the rules of gold check > blue check > normal account. It's still not great, but eventually they added enough slack to let normal accounts with good quips outrank 30 paying users saying "lol", and tweaked some things so it's no longer so easy to shill tshirts/whatever by tagging Grok for the gold check double-boost.

But they're still reticent to ban any Premium account without a reason good enough to give up the $8/month. I have some sympathy for trying to moderate in the era of LLMs that can generate perfectly on-topic replies that even take images into context. But I think they need a more targeted approach against OnlyFans bots replying to popular tweets with a standard formula of some sexual reference and an insane claim. Sometimes they're less sexual and more straight up horrifying [0]:

> i breed mantises for fun and once tried grafting two ooths together just to see what hatched. got a whole clutch of nymphs that all just twitched in circles and died by day two. butterfly chimera energy hits different when it's your own disaster.

The other bot replies to the same OP are the more typical sexualized sort; they tend to reply in swarms.

[0] https://x.com/ariexsha/status/2110924715103514871
children.textZhHtml:
更明显的偏见是高级订阅者而不是我们的贪图便宜者。回复排名算法一度是一场噩梦；他们严格遵守金支票>蓝支票>普通账户的规则。这仍然不是很好，但最终他们增加了足够的宽松度，让普通帐户的好话超过了 30 个说“哈哈”的付费用户，并调整了一些东西，这样就不再那么容易通过标记 Grok 获得金支票双倍提升来推销 T 恤/任何东西。

但他们仍然不愿禁止任何高级帐户，除非有足够好的理由放弃 8 美元/月。我对法学硕士时代的尝试有一些同情，因为法学硕士可以生成完全切中主题的回复，甚至可以将图像融入上下文中。但我认为他们需要一种更有针对性的方法来对付 OnlyFans 机器人，这些机器人用一些性暗示和疯狂主张的标准公式来回复流行的推文。有时它们的性欲更少，更直接令人恐惧[0]：

对同一OP的其他机器人的回复是更典型的性化类型；他们往往会成群地回复。
